Meqabyan (Ethiopian tradition) First Book of Meqabyan (Mäṣḥafä Mäqabyan I) (c. 600 AD)

OPENS Ch 21 — HOMILETIC-GENRE ANCHOR: faithfulness-under-threat theme. The chapter likely develops the Maqabean-martyrs' faithfulness as MODEL for everyday-believer faithfulness — paralleling the 2 Mq Ch 6 mother's-exhortation + 3 Mq Ch 6 suffering-and-perseverance themes (γ.4.8.C + γ.4.8.D entries). Direct biblical parallels: 1 PETER 4:12-19 (Petrine suffering-theology); HEBREWS 10:32-39 (need-of-patience + faith-toward-saving-of-the-soul); REVELATION 2:10 ('be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life'); 2 TIMOTHY 2:11-13 ('if we suffer, we shall also reign with him; if we deny him, he also will deny us'); 1 MACCABEES 2:50-64 (Mattathias's deathbed-exhortation to faithfulness). Patristic-tradition: TERTULLIAN De Fuga in Persecutione (the flee-or-stand-firm controversy); ORIGEN Exhortation to Martyrdom; AUGUSTINE Letter 185 (the political-theology of faithful-resistance). Tewahedo confessional-tradition preserves faithfulness-unto-death as one of the four-cardinal-Christian-virtues (faith + hope + charity + faithfulness — Tewahedo expansion of the Pauline-three).

Meqabyan (Ethiopian tradition) First Book of Meqabyan (Mäṣḥafä Mäqabyan I) (c. 600 AD)

HOMILETIC-GENRE ANCHOR — likely development of WISDOM-SPEECH-PATTERN. The wisdom-speech-pattern parallels: PROVERBS 1-9 (the father-to-son wisdom-instruction format); SIRACH 1-23 (the wisdom-exhortation pattern); WISDOM OF SOLOMON 1-9 (the Solomonic-wisdom-speech pattern); 4 MACCABEES 1:1-3:18 (philosophical-exhortation treatise-form); JAMES 1:5 + 3:13-18 (wisdom-from-above); 1 CORINTHIANS 2:6-16 (Pauline-wisdom from God). Patristic-tradition: AMBROSE De Officiis (modeled on Cicero's De Officiis as Christian-wisdom-treatise); JOHN CHRYSOSTOM De Sacerdotio (pastoral-wisdom-treatise); GREGORY OF NYSSA De Vita Moysis (Moses-as-wisdom-exemplar). Tewahedo wisdom-literature preserves the homiletic-wisdom-treatise as the Mäṣḥafä Tabaqato (Book of the Wise) framework. The Meqabyan chapter likely articulates a wisdom-speech grounded in the post-martyrdom moral-theology established by the trilogy's first two books.
